1.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the revisionist account described in the passage?

options.A: Guild-made goods consistently commanded higher prices than comparable goods produced outside the system, even when independent inspectors judged the two to be of similar quality.
options.B: Many guilds fined members who publicly criticized the quality of a rival master's work, treating such complaints as a threat to the collective reputation of the entire trade.
options.C: Guild statutes routinely required masters to teach apprentices any newly developed technique, and such techniques spread faster within guild towns than beyond them.
options.D: In guild towns the number of licensed masters stayed nearly constant for decades even as the surrounding population grew, leaving many trained journeymen without workshops of their own.

2.stem: The passage implies that high voter turnout counts as evidence of irrationality only if one assumes that

options.A: the only thing a voter values is the instrumental effect of her own ballot.
options.B: the time and effort voting requires always outweigh its rewards.
options.C: a rational agent should disregard the probability that her vote proves decisive.
options.D: voters do not realize how unlikely a single ballot is to be decisive.

3.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the linguist's proposal?

options.A: Whistled communication carried across greater distances than shouting.
options.B: Listeners who had never learned the spoken language, whatever their musical training, could not interpret the whistles at all.
options.C: Untrained but fluent listeners correctly identified whether whistled sentences were questions or statements.
options.D: Trained whistlers could reproduce any spoken sentence in whistled form.

4.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the passage's central claim?

options.A: Improved sanitation over the past century coincided with rising rates of allergy.
options.B: Children raised on farms with varied animal contact had lower allergy rates than urban children with comparable hygiene practices.
options.C: Children in households that washed less frequently had lower allergy rates than other children, even when their contact with animals and older siblings was the same.
options.D: Exposure to a single common bacterium in infancy prevented most allergies.

5.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the step-counting explanation over the alternatives the skeptics raise?

options.A: Stilted ants carried part of the way home overshot their nests by a smaller margin than stilted ants that walked the whole way.
options.B: Stilted ants tested in a tunnel that held the sweep of the visual scene constant overshot their nests by the same margin as stilted ants in the open.
options.C: Ants whose legs were shortened moved more slowly over a given distance than untreated ants did.
options.D: Ants walking home over a strongly patterned surface arrive more accurately than ants walking over a uniform one.

6.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the linguists' hypothesis?

options.A: Listeners identified both the vowel-differing and the consonant-differing pairs with equally high accuracy.
options.B: Speakers found the vowel-differing pairs harder to whistle than the consonant-differing pairs, producing them less consistently.
options.C: Listeners distinguished the vowel-differing pairs far more accurately than the consonant-differing pairs.
options.D: Listeners identified whistled words considerably more slowly than they identified the same words spoken aloud.

7.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the sentence 'Foragers were not innocent of hierarchy; they policed it'?

options.A: It crystallizes the passage's central revision: that equality was actively maintained rather than merely given.
options.B: It introduces evidence that undermines the reliability of ethnographic methods.
options.C: It restates the traditional claim that social hierarchy is natural and inevitable.
options.D: It concedes that foraging societies, for all their leveling techniques, were ultimately as hierarchical as the societies that followed them.

8.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the argument advanced in the text?

options.A: Resource windfalls have been shown to weaken the institutions of countries that were well governed before a discovery.
options.B: Countries with strong institutions tend to have more diversified economies than countries dependent on a single export such as oil or minerals.
options.C: A nation whose institutions were rated weak before an oil discovery continued to grow slowly even after the oil was depleted and the windfall had ended.
options.D: In several countries, growth rates fell sharply in the years immediately following a major mineral discovery.

9.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the historian's claim about how the press spread the Reformation?

options.A: Printed Bibles were most abundant in the cities that had the highest adult literacy rates.
options.B: Catholic authorities also commissioned printed broadsides to circulate their own counterarguments.
options.C: Reformation tracts sold more copies than any earlier genre of printed book.
options.D: In the regions where Reformation ideas spread most rapidly, adult literacy rarely exceeded fifteen percent.

10.stem: Based on the texts, a proponent of the Text 1 explanation could best counter Text 2 by emphasizing which point?

options.A: Text 2's account, though successful for individual galaxies, fails to explain the larger-scale phenomena that dark matter accommodates.
options.B: MOND requires far more adjustable parameters than the dark-matter hypothesis does.
options.C: Dark matter has been directly observed, whereas MOND's proposed modification has not.
options.D: MOND cannot reproduce the observed rotation curves of individual galaxies as accurately as dark-matter halo models can across a wide range of galaxy types.

11.stem: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the passage?

options.A: It contends that native species are, as a general rule, less beneficial to an altered habitat than the non-native species being removed.
options.B: It complicates a conservation principle by arguing that a species' origin is a poor proxy for its actual ecological effect.
options.C: It advocates deliberately introducing non-native species into degraded habitats where the native plants that once held the soil have vanished.
options.D: It defends the orthodox practice of removing every introduced species, on the ground that a non-native plant is a threat wherever it takes hold.

12.stem: Which choice best captures the main point of the passage?

options.A: Wealthy collectors accepted printed volumes only once scribes had filled the blank spaces with decorated initials.
options.B: The printing press mattered chiefly because it invented the title page, the page number, and standardized type.
options.C: Early printed books gained acceptance by imitating manuscripts before developing distinct conventions of their own.
options.D: Printed volumes remained technically inferior to handwritten ones until title pages and standardized type appeared.

13.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the passage's characterization of microcredit's benefit?

options.A: Borrowers with microloans were no more likely than non-borrowers to raise their annual income but were better able to cover irregular, lumpy expenses.
options.B: Regions served by many microfinance institutions had lower overall poverty rates a decade later than otherwise similar regions where such lenders stayed scarce.
options.C: Microloan borrowers reported greater trust in formal financial institutions after repayment, and were likelier than non-borrowers to open a savings account.
options.D: Households that received microloans started markedly more new businesses than otherwise similar households that received no loans.

14.stem: Which choice best describes the village's understanding of wealth?

options.A: Prestige came from giving wealth away rather than from accumulating it.
options.B: Families competed to bring in the largest possible seasonal catch.
options.C: Households that gave away too much were pitied for their poverty.
options.D: Wealth was valued mainly as a secure store against future shortages.

15.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the author would characterize the insulation hypothesis as

options.A: fundamentally mistaken, since feathers show no genuine link to thermoregulation.
options.B: the strongest available explanation for the origin of the complex vaned feathers.
options.C: irrelevant to flight, since ornament rather than warmth produced the earliest feathers.
options.D: accurate for simple filaments but not for the complex feathers that flight required.

16.stem: Which choice is best supported by the text?

options.A: Frost rings form whenever the temperature drops below freezing, including during a tree's dormant winter.
options.B: Most tree rings are hard to date precisely because crushed, discolored cells obscure the bands.
options.C: A frost ring can help researchers determine the part of the year in which a freeze damaged a tree.
options.D: Trees that develop frost rings put on less wood over the season than undamaged trees do.

17.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text's reasoning about a manuscript that lacks a particular shared error?

options.A: It contains no copying errors of any kind, having been transcribed faithfully.
options.B: It was necessarily copied at an earlier date than any surviving manuscript containing that error.
options.C: It did not descend, even indirectly, from the flawed exemplar that introduced that error.
options.D: It served as the exemplar from which every other surviving manuscript was ultimately copied.

18.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly undermine the assumption on which the therapeutic proposal rests?

options.A: The reconsolidation-blocking drug reduces the memory's emotional charge immediately after treatment and for several days after the session.
options.B: Different reconsolidation-blocking drugs disrupt the process to different degrees, and none of them blocks it completely in every patient.
options.C: After the drug is given, the original memory reappears intact following a delay, implying the drug disrupted only a newly formed copy.
options.D: Memories formed long ago are generally harder to reactivate in the laboratory than memories formed recently, whatever drug is later given.

19.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the psychologist's claim?

options.A: Of the 200 workers with fixed schedules, 132 reported high satisfaction, compared with only 76 of the 200 with flexible schedules.
options.B: Of the 200 workers with flexible schedules, 132 reported high satisfaction, compared with 76 of the 200 with fixed schedules.
options.C: Of the 200 workers with flexible schedules, 68 reported low satisfaction rather than high satisfaction.
options.D: Equal numbers of flexible- and fixed-schedule workers, 132 in each group, reported high satisfaction.

20.stem: The text suggests that Wegener's critics rejected continental drift primarily because

options.A: seafloor spreading already offered a more convincing account of the same evidence.
options.B: they refused on principle to weigh any evidence that unsettled the geology they had been taught as students.
options.C: he had documented striking correlations but could not identify a force capable of producing them.
options.D: his matching coastlines and shared fossils were later shown to have been misidentified.

21.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the archaeologist's argument?

options.A: The animal bones and plant remains on the floors come exclusively from species available only in the warm months.
options.B: Stone structures of similar size and construction elsewhere in the region were occupied by their builders all year.
options.C: The structures sit in a tight cluster on the hillside rather than spread along its slope.
options.D: The structures were built from stone quarried at an outcrop several kilometers down the valley.

22.stem: Which statement about Titian's late works is best supported by the passage?

options.A: Their appeal to modern viewers proves that Titian consciously anticipated modern painting.
options.B: Their loose handling reflects a mix of deliberate effects and passages Titian never brought to completion.
options.C: Contemporaries failed to appreciate the freedom of his late touch.
options.D: Their rough surfaces were entirely the product of external constraints rather than artistic intent.

23.stem: How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the 'settled' view described in Text 1?

options.A: By arguing that the textbook prediction assumes a market structure that low-wage labor may not fit
options.B: By maintaining that the law of demand is simply false when applied to labor markets
options.C: By noting that New Jersey's wage increase was too small to affect any hiring decisions
options.D: By conceding that minimum wage increases always reduce employment, as the textbooks claim

24.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

options.A: records observation at its own house rather than transmission of the northern figures.
options.B: was copied from the northern table and afterward corrected by a later reader.
options.C: contains a systematic error of about forty minutes introduced in the course of copying.
options.D: rests on observations gathered over a longer span of time than the northern table's.
